title: The Strongest Lock
about: Some second locks are harder to steal than others. Pick the strongest.

cards.situation: Mia's email asks her to make a passkey. She's never heard of one.

image.alt: Mia holds her phone. A pop-up over her inbox asks "Sign in faster with a passkey?" with two buttons, Make a passkey and Not now. A question mark floats over Mia's head.

cards.prompt: Mia's email offers three locks. **Tap** each to see how it works.

parts.job: A code comes by text message. You type it in.
An app on your phone makes the code. Nothing is sent.
Your phone checks your face, fingerprint or PIN. No code to type.

cards.explanation: Three locks: a code by text, a code from an app, or your face, fingerprint or PIN.

cards.prompt: The scammer has Mia's password, and now her number. What happens?

image.alt: Mia's Sign-in options screen with three choices, Text me a code, Authenticator app and Passkey, each with a shut padlock. Far away, a scammer holds a second phone tagged Mia's number, as a text message arrives on it.
image.revealAlt: The Text me a code padlock breaks open: its code, 481 902, goes to the scammer's phone. The Authenticator app and Passkey padlocks stay shut.

cards.explanation: Only the text code travels to Mia's number, so the other two locks hold.

cards.title: Three locks, ranked
cards.body: Strongest to weakest: a **passkey**, an **authenticator app**, then a text code. Any of them beats a password alone.

image.alt: A podium: Passkey stands in first place, Authenticator app in second and Text code in third. A grey, dashed key labelled Password alone lies on the floor beside it.

cards.prompt: Mia lines up four ways to sign in. Drag them strongest to weakest.
cards.explanation: Spot on: each one is harder to steal than the one under it.
cards.nudge: Start at the bottom: which one has no second lock at all?
cards.showAnswer: Passkey, then authenticator app, then text code, then a password alone, with no second lock.

cards.prompt: A fake email page asks for Mia's password and code. Which lock keeps her safe?

image.alt: A laptop shows a page that looks just like Mia's email sign-in, with a Password box and a Code box. An amber tag on its corner says Fake copy. A scammer peeks out from behind the screen. Mia's phone sits beside it.
image.revealAlt: Mia's phone says No passkey for this site. The fake page's Password and Code boxes stay empty, and the scammer shrugs.

cards.explanation: Yes: a passkey only works on the real site, so the fake copy gets nothing.
cards.nudge: If Mia types a code into this page, who sees it?
cards.showAnswer: The passkey: any code Mia types goes to the fake page, but a passkey only works on the real site.

cards.prompt: Your music app only offers text codes. Turn on two-step sign-in?

image.alt: Your phone shows a music app's Two-step sign-in setting with one option, Text me a code, switched off. Far away, a scammer with your password types it into a laptop.
image.revealAlt: The Text me a code switch is now on. Far away, the scammer is stuck at Enter the code.

options.text: Yes: a weak lock beats no lock
No: text codes can be stolen

cards.explanation: Right: most scammers only have a password, and a text code stops them.
cards.nudge: Which is harder to get into: a password plus a text code, or a password alone?
cards.showAnswer: Turn it on: any second lock beats a password alone, and you can switch to a better one later.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
Use the strongest lock an app offers: passkey, then authenticator app, then text code. Any beats none.

**Try this:** With a trusted adult, or on your own if you're 18+, look in one app's settings for a passkey or authenticator app.

**Next:** The scam email that pretends to be someone you trust.
